Our ability to quantify the envionmental intangibles which are perhaps the dominant costs and benefits of an endangered species program is still rudimentary. To what degree the maintenance of biological complexity and     ecological diversity is related to environmental productivity and stability, for example, is unknown, although such a relationship is well documented. The potential for any species, currently endangered or not, to produce future knowledge, substances, or economic opportunity of ecological, medical or recreational value is impossible to quantify. It is similarly impossible to document the cash value of endangered species publicity to the recreation industry in sale of supplies and services relating to nature activities. How many binoculars are sold to those awakened to bird watching by the sight of a well-publicized bald eagle? How many miles are driven, how many motel rooms occupied, by hopeful seekers for the ivory-billed woodpecker? A significant proportion of the benefits, and costs, of this program are of such a nature and we are not now, and may never be, able to resolve this problem.
Until such time as the ability to resolve this difficulty becomes available we are constrained to deal only in qualitative terms. The remainder of this section will follow this approach.
The Secretary now lists nearly 500 species as endangered worldwide and within the United States. Authority under the proposed legislation would considerably expand the number of species and subspecies eligible for designation as endangered species as well as strengthen provisions available to the Secretary to manage, protect, and restore those species.
